blocks.text: 1. Average Pooling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341148-12584392.png

Max Pooling, the previous topic, kept only the largest value within each pooling window. Average Pooling is a complete, dedicated look at Pooling's other common variant, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
It works by averaging every value within each small window, rather than keeping just the largest, a genuinely different summarization philosophy covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. The Rule
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341148-4568893.png
This connects back to the pooling window, already covered in Pooling. At each position, examine every value inside that small window, following the same sliding pattern already covered there.
Compute their genuinely simple average, rather than the maximum already covered in Max Pooling, a genuinely direct, simple rule that gives Average Pooling its own distinctive name.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Term","Meaning"],"rows":[["Average Pooling","Averaging every value within each small pooling window"],["Max Pooling, already covered","Keeping only the single largest value within each window"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why Average Specifically
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341148-175907395.png

A genuinely intuitive justification connects back to keeping the strongest signal, already covered in Max Pooling. Average Pooling instead genuinely preserves the overall, general level of activation across the entire region.
This makes the average value within a region a genuinely meaningful summary of that region's overall character, rather than focusing on just its single most extreme point.
4. The Smoothing Effect
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341358-584526268.png

This connects back to why average specifically, already covered in this topic. Averaging genuinely smooths out sharp, individual peaks within a region, blending them together into one representative value.

This is a genuinely gentler summary than the single-peak-preserving behavior already covered in Max Pooling, treating every value in the region as genuinely equally important rather than singling out just the maximum.
5. A Genuine Tradeoff: Losing Fine Detail

blocks.alt: A Genuine Tradeoff: Losing Fine Detail
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341359-141011430.png

A genuinely real tradeoff follows. This connects back to keeping the strongest signal, already covered in Max Pooling. Average Pooling can genuinely dilute a strong, sharp signal by blending it with weaker, surrounding values.

This is a genuinely real cost to weigh against the smoothing benefit already covered in the previous section, and it directly explains why Max Pooling remains the genuinely more common default choice for most convolutional layers.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: This dilution effect, already covered in this topic, is exactly why Average Pooling is used less often than Max Pooling between convolutional layers, where preserving sharp, detected features usually matters more.

blocks.text: 6. A Preview Of Global Average Pooling

A genuinely important, related variant, covered later in this module, connects back to Flattening, covered further in this module. Global Average Pooling applies this same averaging idea across an entire feature map at once.

Rather than a small local window, already covered throughout this topic, it averages across the genuinely entire spatial extent of a feature map, a distinctive application explored in complete depth later in this module.
7. Where Networks Typically Use It
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341359-29570664.png

This connects back to typical Convolutional Neural Network architectures, covered further in CNN Architectures. Average Pooling appears less often between convolutional layers than Max Pooling does, echoing the tradeoff already covered earlier in this topic.

It commonly appears near the genuinely end of a network instead, already previewed in this topic as Global Average Pooling, where smoothing and summarizing the entire feature map becomes genuinely more valuable than preserving sharp local detail.
8. Recapping Max Pooling Versus Average Pooling

blocks.alt: Recapping Max Pooling Versus Average Pooling
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445341359-154588224.png

This connects back to Max Pooling versus a preview of Average Pooling, already covered in Max Pooling. Max Pooling keeps the genuinely strongest signal, preserving sharp features detected anywhere within a region.

Average Pooling smooths across the region instead, preserving genuinely overall, general context rather than any single sharp peak, the direct, complete contrast already previewed in the previous topic.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Average Pooling Is Genuinely The Right Choice

Wanting a genuinely smooth, general summary of an entire region rather than its single peak is a direct case for Average Pooling, since it, already covered in this topic, directly delivers exactly that.

This connects forward to Global Average Pooling, covered later in this module, at a network's genuinely final stage, where Average Pooling's own smoothing philosophy, already covered, extends naturally there.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates Average Pooling's core computation, applying a 2x2 window with stride 2 to the exact same feature map already used in Max Pooling, contrasting the results.

code.content:
import numpy as np

feature_map = np.array([
    [1, 3, 2, 4],
    [5, 6, 1, 2],
    [7, 2, 9, 4],
    [3, 1, 0, 8],
])  # the exact same feature map already used in Max Pooling's worked example

pool_size = 2
stride = 2

output_size = (feature_map.shape[0] - pool_size) // stride + 1
avg_pooled = np.zeros((output_size, output_size))

for i in range(output_size):
    for j in range(output_size):
        row, col = i * stride, j * stride
        region = feature_map[row:row + pool_size, col:col + pool_size]
        avg_pooled[i, j] = region.mean()  # already covered as the rule in this topic

print("Original feature map:\n", feature_map)
print("\nAverage pooled output:\n", avg_pooled)
print("\nCompare this to Max Pooling's output on the same feature map: notice the values here are genuinely smoother, already covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example on the exact same feature map already used in Max Pooling shows genuinely smoother, less extreme output values here, exactly the smoothing effect already covered as this topic's own core mechanism.

blocks.text: 11. Convolutional Neural Networks: Progress Recap

items: Average Pooling averages every value within each small pooling window, rather than keeping just the largest.
It preserves the overall, general level of activation across a region, rather than a single peak.
Averaging smooths out sharp, individual peaks within a region.
It can dilute a strong, sharp signal by blending it with weaker, surrounding values.
Global Average Pooling, covered later in this module, extends this same idea across an entire feature map.
It appears less often between convolutional layers than Max Pooling, but commonly appears near a network's end.
Max Pooling preserves sharp features; Average Pooling preserves overall, general context.
